draft.title: Global health inequities
card: Global health inequities are unfair differences in health between countries. Life expectancy, the average number of years a person is expected to live, can differ by decades between rich and poor countries.
Poverty is a major driver. Poorer households and countries have less money for food, housing, medicines and health services.
Clean water and sanitation (safe toilets and waste disposal) help stop infectious diseases such as diarrhoea from spreading. Where they are missing, more people fall ill and die young.
Education and access to care also shape health. Education helps people understand how to stay well, and access to care means illness can be prevented or treated early.
draft.remember: Gaps in life expectancy between countries are linked to poverty, unsafe water and sanitation, less education and poor access to care.

a.q: Which statement best describes a global health inequity?
opts: People in some countries can expect to live decades less
People in every country face the same illnesses equally
Older people in all countries have shorter lives than youth
Countries with more doctors always have fewer infections
a.why: A global health inequity is an unfair gap in health between countries, such as life expectancy differing by decades. The last option is tempting, but the card does not say more doctors always mean fewer infections.
a.clue: Think of an unfair gap in health between countries.

b.q: A village has no safe toilets, and its creek is the only drinking water. Children there often get severe diarrhoea. Which explanation fits best?
opts: Missing clean water and sanitation lets infection spread
Low life expectancy is caused only by a lack of education
Diarrhoea is mainly a problem of countries with more money
Medicines are the only way to lower the spread of infection
b.why: Without safe water and sanitation, infectious diseases spread easily, which can lower life expectancy. Education and access to care also matter, but the case describes water and toilets, so the tempting option that blames education alone is wrong.
b.clue: Look at what the village lacks, not at what it could buy.

a.best: People in some countries can expect to live decades less

b.best: Missing clean water and sanitation lets infection spread

problems.detail: The three wrong options all use absolute words ('always', 'every', 'equally', 'all'), while the right option has none. A student can pick it by rejecting the absolutes without knowing the idea.
Why (a) calls the doctors option 'the last option', but the options are shuffled, so the position is wrong and confusing. It also never explains why the other two distractors are wrong.
The wrong options use 'only' (twice) and 'mainly', while the right option is the only one without an absolute or limiting word. This makes it easy to spot by elimination.
The clue 'Look at what the village lacks' points straight to the only option that begins with 'Missing', giving the answer away.

a.q: Which statement describes a global health inequity?
opts: People in poorer countries can expect to live decades less
Older people in a country have fewer years left than youth
Two neighbours in one Sydney suburb eat different diets
A country's health care spending rises from year to year
a.why: A global health inequity is an unfair gap in health between countries, such as life expectancy differing by decades. Older people having fewer years left is a natural part of ageing within one country, not an unfair gap between countries. Neighbours' diets are personal choices in one suburb, and rising spending describes a budget, not a health difference.
a.clue: Look for an unfair health gap between countries.

b.q: A village has no safe toilets, and its creek is the only drinking water. Children there often get severe diarrhoea. Which explanation fits best?
opts: Unsafe water and no toilets let infection spread
The children were born with weak immune systems
Repeated illness in the children made the creek unsafe
Living far from a city makes creek water unsafe
b.why: Without clean water and sanitation, waste can get into drinking water and infectious diseases such as diarrhoea spread easily. Blaming the illness for the unsafe creek is tempting, but it reverses cause and effect: the missing toilets and unsafe water come first. Distance from a city does not make water unsafe, and nothing in the case points to an inborn weakness.
b.clue: Think about how diarrhoea passes from person to person.
